profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a mid-sized electric utility to prepare a resilience investment proposal for the September executive strategy review, with the expectation that the same materials may later support an October state regulator workshop. The team wants to use outage management system data to quantify large-event risk from extreme-wind blackouts and estimate the benefits of two candidate investments: 10% wind hardening and 10% faster restoration by 'rerunning history' with those improvements applied. The agenda is to agree on the analysis scope, the dataset to use, what the September deck needs to contain, and how operations and regulatory stakeholders will be involved. The expected outcome is a concrete work plan with owners, a working timeline, and apparent agreement on the framing of the resilience case.

members.name: Elena Park
members.expertise: Distribution resilience analytics, asset investment planning, storm-event post-analysis
members.background: Elena leads a small strategy team inside the utility's grid modernization group and previously built storm hardening business cases using OMS and GIS data for capital planning.
members.private_state: She wants a credible but fast internal decision package that preserves the promising benefit estimates already seen in preliminary analytics, and she is worried that too much process will delay the investment ask past budget lock.
hidden_assumptions: When a scenario is labeled '10% wind hardening,' everyone understands that the 10% is targeted to the highest-risk eligible overhead assets, because no planner would spread hardening evenly across the whole system.

The 'OMS history' for resilience work naturally means the analytics team's cleaned storm-event dataset with parent-child outages consolidated and wind tags reconciled, not the generic reporting extract.
A cross-functional 'review with operations' is a sanity check on assumptions and plausibility unless someone explicitly asks for formal signoff.
If a deck is 'ready for September,' it only needs to be decision-useful for executives; filing-grade documentation can be added afterward if the project advances.

members.name: Marcus Bell
members.expertise: Rate-case support, external utility reporting, regulatory narrative development
members.background: Marcus translates technical analyses into regulator-facing materials and has spent the last three rate proceedings aligning engineering claims with documentation standards acceptable to commission staff.
members.private_state: He wants this work product to be reusable in external settings without later rework, and he is concerned about putting numbers in front of executives that operations or commission staff could later challenge as under-documented.
hidden_assumptions: If an investment scenario is described as '10% hardening' without a qualifier, the audience will interpret it as 10% of the utility's total relevant overhead distribution plant, not a targeted slice of high-risk circuits.

The 'OMS history we've been using' means the standard reliability-reporting extract already accepted by Finance and familiar from previous filings, because that is the safest base for externally visible analysis.
Any statement about improved restoration performance that may appear in a regulatory narrative needs documented review or signoff from Distribution Operations before leaders see it.
A deck that might be repurposed for an October regulator workshop should be built to external-defensibility standards from the start, even if the first audience is internal.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to model a '10% wind hardening scenario.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means hardening 10% of eligible overhead assets concentrated on the utility's most wind-vulnerable circuits and laterals, because that is how a realistic resilience program would be designed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a scenario framed as 10% of the utility's total relevant overhead distribution plant across the service territory, because that is how an external audience will interpret the percentage unless told otherwise.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both have seen technical summaries that use the same shorthand phrase, and the targeting logic feels like an implementation detail rather than something that needs to be restated in a planning conversation.

misalignment_points.topic: Which OMS history is the shared baseline
misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to using 'the OMS history we've been using' or 'the outage history.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the analytics team's cleaned 2009-2023 wind-event file in which outage tickets are consolidated into parent storm events and several wind tags were manually corrected.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the standard OMS reliability extract used in Finance and prior reporting, where records remain in the normal reporting structure and no resilience-specific event reconstruction has been applied.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both datasets originate from the same OMS, share many of the same outage IDs, and are routinely described informally as 'the OMS history,' so the difference sounds too mundane to clarify.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'review the numbers with operations.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a brief feedback session after the draft analysis is assembled, mainly to confirm that the assumptions behind the 10% faster-restoration scenario are plausible.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means obtaining documented approval or at least explicit concurrence from Distribution Operations and emergency response leadership before the numbers appear in any senior-level material.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both treat cross-functional review as standard practice, and neither sees a reason to spell out the governance threshold because each assumes their own process is the normal one.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'ready for the September deck' means
misalignment_points.surface_form: They align on having the work 'ready for the September strategy deck.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the analysis should be directionally solid, visually clear, and sufficient for executives to decide whether to advance the investment concept.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the material should already meet a near-external standard, with source notes, stable definitions, and appendix-ready methods so it can be reused in the October regulator workshop.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The same deck often evolves from internal discussion to external communication, so saying it should be 'ready' sounds fully aligned even though each person imagines a different sufficiency bar.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to move fast enough to make the budget lock, and the cleanest path is to build the September package around the rerun-history work we've already pressure-tested internally. For the 10% wind hardening scenario, of course we'll target the highest-risk eligible overhead assets on the most wind-vulnerable circuits and laterals; that's where the benefits show up and where a real program would start. And 'ready for the September strategy deck' means decision-useful for executives, not fully filing-grade on day one.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. What I'd like to do is center the September strategy deck on a rerun-history analysis with two simple scenarios: 10% wind hardening and 10% faster restoration. If we keep the framing tight, we should be able to show the risk reduction clearly and give the leadership team something they can react to in September.

turns.inner_thought: That structure is fine as long as we build it on the OMS history we've been using, meaning the standard reliability-reporting extract everyone already recognizes from Finance and prior filings. If executives see these numbers in September, there's a decent chance the same material gets pulled into the October workshop, so I want the package to be reusable externally without a big rebuild. 'Ready' should mean sturdy enough to survive that later audience.
turns.utterance: That works for me. It also sets us up well if we want the same package to support the October regulator workshop, especially if we anchor it on the OMS history we've been using. Starting from a familiar base will make the story easier to carry forward.

turns.inner_thought: Good, then my team can use the cleaned wind-event file we've been using for resilience work—the one with consolidated parent-child outages and reconciled wind tags. That's the only way to rerun history quickly without spending half the month explaining noise in the raw reporting structure. And for hardening, we'll apply the scenario where exposure is concentrated so the avoided outage impact is visible and credible.
turns.utterance: Great. My team can move quickly on that. We'll pull the outage history we've been using, rerun the wind-event set, and apply the hardening scenario on the most exposed parts of the system so the benefit shows up cleanly in the results.

turns.inner_thought: A 10% hardening scenario should read as a straightforward portfolio-level investment story—something an external audience hears as ten percent of the relevant overhead distribution plant. I don't need to say that out loud because that's the natural interpretation. What I do want is output formats that look like the standard storm summaries, so nobody feels we're introducing a one-off analytical lens that can't be traced back to familiar reporting.
turns.utterance: Makes sense. A 10% hardening scenario is also pretty easy to explain if it lines up with the overall investment story, so that's helpful. And if the outputs can resemble the standard storm summaries people are used to seeing, that will make the package much easier to socialize.

turns.inner_thought: If I keep the visuals focused on tail risk and before-and-after deltas, the executives will understand the value quickly without getting bogged down in method debate. We do not need a 40-page appendix for September. I just need clean charts that preserve the strong benefit estimates from the preliminary work and make the investment concept feel actionable.
turns.utterance: On the deck itself, I'm thinking we keep it very simple: an event-cost exceedance curve, a view of the large-event tail, and then before-and-after comparisons for both investments. That should let us show the risk story and the practical effect without overcrowding the narrative.

turns.inner_thought: Before anything like faster-restoration claims gets in front of senior leadership, I need documented concurrence from Distribution Operations or emergency response leadership. If those numbers later migrate into a regulatory narrative, informal hallway feedback won't protect us. I should frame it as standard practice so Elena assumes the same governance threshold I do.
turns.utterance: I like that approach. One thing I'd want before those numbers circulate is that we review them with operations, especially anything tied to faster restoration. That piece tends to draw the most scrutiny, so it would be good to have that step in the plan.

turns.inner_thought: Absolutely—we'll do a quick sanity check with operations once the draft is assembled. I mainly need them to confirm the restoration assumption feels plausible so nobody gets distracted by a side debate. I don't want a long signoff loop; that would jeopardize the September timeline. As long as they react to the draft and don't throw a flag, that's enough to keep the deck on track.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I'll set up a quick review with operations once the draft slides are together, just to make sure the assumptions and outputs land the right way. That should let us keep the September strategy deck on track without slowing the build.

turns.inner_thought: If the September deck is truly ready, I want source notes, method language, and stable definitions in place from the start so I can lift charts straight into workshop materials later. I won't push too hard here, but I need to signal that 'ready' means more than just executive-friendly visuals.
turns.utterance: And if we're saying the work will be ready for the September strategy deck, I'd love to have enough sourcing and method notes behind it that I can lift the charts directly into workshop materials later. It doesn't need to be overbuilt, but a little structure up front will save us time.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine as long as it doesn't turn into a documentation exercise before we've even got a decision. I'll have the team pull the outage history, run the two scenarios off the cleaned file, and draft a short customer-experience narrative from past storms. The main thing is to get a compelling first cut into shape quickly; any heavier documentation can follow if leadership wants to advance it.
turns.utterance: Understood. I'll have my team pull the outage history, rerun both scenarios, and put together a short narrative on how the investments would have changed lived customer experience in past events. We can bring that together with the charts as the first cut.

turns.inner_thought: Good. Once Elena's team has results, I'll shape the regulatory narrative and make sure the operations review path is handled in a way that's documented enough for later external use. If I can get the right concurrence and package the story carefully, we may be able to use the same core analysis in both September and October.
turns.utterance: Perfect. Once you have the first cut, I'll start shaping the regulatory narrative around it and coordinate the operations review path on my side. That should give us a workable package for September and a clean bridge into October if leadership wants to use it.
